'''''Drosera intermedia''''', commonly known as the '''oblong-leaved sundew''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''spoonleaf sundew''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=DRIN3|taxon=Drosera intermedia|accessdate=18 January 2016}}</ref> or '''spatulate leaved sundew''', is an [[carnivorous plant|insectivorous plant]] species belonging to the [[sundew]] [[genus]]. It is a [[temperate]] or [[tropical]] species native to [[Europe]], southeastern [[Canada]], the eastern half of the [[United States]], [[Cuba]], [[Hispaniola]], and northern [[South America]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Search |url=https://www.gbif.org/occurrence/search?taxon_key=3191157 |access-date=2022-07-18 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Description==
''Drosera intermedia'' is a perennial [[herb]] which forms a semi-erect stemless rosette of spatulate leaves up to 10 cm tall. Plants in temperate regions undergo [[dormancy]] during which they form a winter resting bud called a [[Hibernaculum (botany)|hibernaculum]].

As is typical for [[sundew]]s, the leaf blades are densely covered with stalked [[mucilage|mucilaginous]] glands which secrete a sugary nectar to attract insects. These then become ensnared by the mucilage and, unless they are strong enough to escape, are suffocated or die from exhaustion. The plant then secretes digestive enzymes from [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] glands and later absorbs the resulting nutrient solution to supplement the poor mineral nutrition of the plants natural environment.

''Drosera intermedia'' blooms from June through August, forming up to 15 cm. tall [[inflorescence]]s bearing 3–8 white [[flower]]s. Fertilized ovaries swell to form egg-shaped dehiscent seed capsules which bear numerous tiny seeds.{{Citation needed|date=May 2025}}

==Distribution and habitat==
''Drosera intermedia'' is one of the most widely distributed species in the genus, and one of only three ''[[Drosera]]'' species native to [[Europe]] (the others are ''[[Drosera rotundifolia|D. rotundifolia]]'' and ''[[Drosera anglica|D. anglica]]''). It is also found in eastern North America, [[Cuba]], and northern South America. The Cuban and South American forms are tropical and do not form [[Hibernaculum (botany)|hibernacula]] in the winter.{{Citation needed|date=May 2025}}

''Drosera intermedia'' grows in sunny, but constantly moist habitats including bogs, fens,<ref>Godwin, K. S., Shallenberger, J., Leopold, D. J., and Bedford, B. L. 2002. Linking landscape properties to local hydrogeologic gradients and plant species occurrence in New York fens: a hydrogeologic setting (HGS) framework. Wetlands 22:722–37.</ref> wet sandy shorelines<ref>Keddy, P.A. 1981.  Vegetation with Atlantic coastal plain affinities in Axe Lake, near Georgian Bay, Ontario.  Canadian Field-Naturalist 95: 241–248.</ref> and [[wet meadow]]s.  Since it is carnivorous, it is able to occupy relatively infertile habitats including wet sand and peat. It is a relatively weak competitor, and so is excluded from more fertile sites by competition from canopy-forming perennials.<ref>Wilson, S. D. and P.A. Keddy.  1986.  Species competitive ability and position along a natural stress/disturbance gradient.  Ecology 67:1236–1242.</ref> It can survive high water periods as buried seeds, and then re-establish when water levels fall.<ref>Keddy, P.A. and A. A. Reznicek. 1982.  The role of seed banks in the persistence of Ontario's coastal plain flora.  American Journal of Botany 69:13–22.</ref>
